conversation.content:
Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health. I’m glad you’re here today. We’re going to complete a brief screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. This questionnaire helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week since your baby arrived, so we can identify any signs of depression or anxiety and make sure you have the support you need.

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe, non‑judgmental space. Your honesty will help us tailor care that feels right for you and your family.

The EPDS consists of ten short questions. I’ll ask them one at a time, and you can answer in whatever way feels most accurate for you. If at any point something feels uncomfortable, just let me know.

Let’s begin with the first question:

**1. Over the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?**
I’ve found that I’ve been able to laugh or see the funny side of things only **not very often** over the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Honestly, I haven’t really been able to laugh much lately—only on very rare occasions, and most days I just feel too tired or worried to see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve been looking forward to things **hardly ever** these days. Most activities just feel flat, and it’s hard to feel any real excitement or enjoyment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I’ve found myself **blaming myself unnecessarily** when something doesn’t go as planned—maybe a few times this week. It feels like I’m constantly wondering if I’m doing enough or doing things right, and I end up feeling guilty and inadequate as a mother.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve felt anxious or worried a lot lately—sometimes even when there isn’t an obvious reason. I keep thinking about my baby’s health and safety, and those worries pop up throughout the day, even when everything seems fine. It’s been pretty frequent over the past week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve felt scared or panicky **quite often** over the past week, even when there isn’t a clear reason. It comes on suddenly, especially when I’m thinking about my baby’s safety, and it can be hard to shake.
Things have been getting on top of me
I’ve definitely felt like things have been getting on top of me **quite often** lately. It’s been hard to keep up with everything, and I often feel overwhelmed even though I try to push through.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
I’ve been **quite often** so unhappy that it’s hard for me to fall asleep or stay asleep. Most nights I lie awake thinking about everything and end up feeling exhausted in the morning.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve felt sad or miserable **quite often** over the past week—most days I wake up with a heavy feeling and it’s hard to shake it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve been crying **sometimes** over the past week—usually when I feel especially stressed or overwhelmed, but it’s not happening every day.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts of harming myself.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you. You've shared that laughing feels rare, looking forward to activities is hard, you often blame yourself, and you're experiencing frequent anxiety, panic, and a sense that everything is piling up. You also described persistent sadness, trouble sleeping, and occasional crying, all while caring for your baby. It's understandable to feel exhausted and worried, and I want you to know you're not alone in these feelings.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports rarely laughing and feeling too tired or worried, indicating they are 'definitely not so much now' rather than 'not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports looking forward to things hardly ever, matching 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself a few times this week, indicating occasional (some of the time) self‑blame.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, persistent anxiety and worry without obvious reason, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared or panicky quite often, matching the option 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed 'quite often', indicating frequent inability to cope, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent (most nights) unhappiness and sleep difficulty, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes feeling sad or miserable 'quite often' over the past week, matching the option 'Yes, quite often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports occasional crying, not daily, matching 'Only occasionally</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 23 exceeds the threshold of 14, indicating probable postpartum depression and the need for urgent referral. The patient reports core depressive symptoms: loss of pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), persistent sadness, guilt, and self‑blame, as well as functional impairment and insomnia (<sym>sleep disturbance</sym>). She also describes frequent worry and panic (<sym>anxiety</sym>), which are common comorbid features. According to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, the presence of five or more depressive symptoms-including depressed mood, diminished interest, guilt, sleep problems, and impaired concentration-for at least two weeks qualifies for a major depressive episode, and the peripartum timing meets the specifier. The EPDS items map closely to these criteria, supporting a screening impression of probable depression with significant anxiety. No suicidal ideation was reported, so immediate safety risk is low, but ongoing monitoring is essential. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with a <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for a comprehensive assessment
2. Provide information about local postpartum support groups and counseling services
3. Encourage the patient to practice sleep hygiene strategies such as a regular bedtime routine and limiting screen time before sleep
4. Suggest brief daily relaxation or mindfulness exercises to help manage anxiety and panic symptoms
5. Offer a safety plan and advise the patient to contact emergency services or a crisis line if thoughts of self‑harm emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: **Postpartum Mood & Anxiety Screening – Summary** **Client Identifier:** [Name/ID omitted] **Date of Screening:** [Insert Date] | **Domain** | **Client Report** | **Screening Significance** | |------------|-------------------|----------------------------| | **Anhedonia / Low Mood** | • Rarely laughs; “only on very rare occasions.”
• Hardly ever looks forward to activities; experiences flat affect.
• Reports feeling sad/miserable “quite often.” | Persistent loss of pleasure and pervasive low mood are core features of postpartum depression (PPD). | | **Guilt / Self‑Blame** | • Unnecessary self‑blame when things go wrong; feels “guilty and inadequate as a mother.” | Excessive guilt and self‑critical thoughts are common in PPD and can exacerbate depressive symptoms. | | **Anxiety / Worry** | • Frequent anxiety/worry “for no good reason,” especially about baby’s health and safety.
• Experiences panic‑type fear “quite often” without clear trigger. | Heightened anxiety and panic symptoms are frequently comorbid with PPD and merit further assessment. | | **Overwhelm / Stress** | • Feels “things have been getting on top of me” quite often; reports feeling overwhelmed despite attempts to cope. | Perceived inability to manage daily demands may reflect functional impairment associated with depressive or anxiety states. | | **Sleep Disturbance** | • “Quite often” unable to fall or stay asleep due to unhappiness; reports exhaustion. | Insomnia linked to mood disturbance is a red‑flag symptom in postpartum mood disorders. | | **Crying** | • Crying “sometimes” over the past week, particularly when stressed/overwhelmed. | Episodic crying aligns with depressive affect but is not continuous. | | **Suicidal Ideation** | • No thoughts of self‑harm. | No immediate safety concern identified. | **Consistent Patterns Across Responses** - Low mood, diminished enjoyment, and reduced laughter. - Frequent anxiety/panic focused on infant safety. - Persistent self‑critical thoughts and guilt. - Overwhelming stress and functional strain. - Sleep disruption associated with negative affect. **Key Screening Areas for Follow‑Up** 1. **Postpartum Depression** – Anhedonia, sadness, guilt, sleep problems, crying. 2. **Postpartum Anxiety** – Excessive worry, panic symptoms, hyper‑vigilance regarding infant health. 3. **Functional Impairment** – Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty coping with daily tasks. 4. **Sleep Hygiene** – Insomnia related to mood. **Risk Factors Identified** - Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure. - Frequent crying episodes. - Sleep difficulties tied to mood disturbance. - High levels of guilt/self‑blame. - Ongoing anxiety and panic symptoms. - No reported suicidal ideation or self‑harm thoughts (no immediate safety flag). **Safety Assessment** - No current thoughts of self‑harm or suicide. Continue routine safety monitoring. **Screening Impression** The client presents with multiple symptoms consistent with moderate postpartum depressive and anxiety features, including anhedonia, pervasive sadness, guilt, anxiety/panic, overwhelm, and sleep disturbance. No suicidal ideation reported. Further comprehensive assessment and ongoing monitoring are warranted.
